title: Your AI policy has a hole in it. A sophomore will find it by week two
author: Doan Winkel
source: howtoteachwithai.substack.com (How to Teach With AI), October 16, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel argues that most course AI policies fail in the same seven ways: loopholes in the wording, students who break rules without knowing what counts, honest students who read a threat and stop trying, good use that looks like cheating, detectors that accuse the wrong person, team projects with no rules, and policies nobody can enforce. To test this he built an "AI Policy Board" of ten simulated seats, including a rules lawyer, a Grammarly-reliant student, a falsely flagged student, a TA and an integrity officer, and ran a typical university template through it. The template was rated collapsing by every seat, and the rewrite emerged from rounds of adversarial argument, such as the objection that a blank disclosure line turns into perjury and that disclosure shows compliance but is not compliance. The rebuilt policy cut estimated enforcement time from 23 hours a semester to about seven. He offers a free prompt to run the board in any AI tool and three quick self-check questions, and notes that a policy can be amended mid-semester.
points: Ambiguous wording and a penalty-heavy tone push the most conscientious students to avoid AI entirely, while the rules lawyer simply switches tools.
A policy must say what counts as AI (naming tools like Grammarly) and what happens first when a violation is suspected, rather than pointing to the university handbook.
Adversarial role-play by simulated student and staff seats exposed holes that a single author reading their own policy would miss.
Enforceability is a design constraint: the rebuilt policy cost about seven hours a semester to enforce versus 23 for the original template, with every check fitting in ninety seconds.
Policies should never treat polish, second-language writing or accommodations as grounds for suspicion, and nobody defended AI detectors as evidence.
quotes: Your syllabus says “generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the instructor.” A student used Claude.
The Grammarly Kid has used Grammarly, autocomplete, and the AI answer at the top of Google since ninth grade. She does not think any of it is AI.
The Honest One is the rule-follower you want most. She read your penalties paragraph and turned everything off.
The Honest One wanted disclosed use to never count as academic dishonesty. The integrity officer shut that down in five words: “Disclosure shows compliance. It is not compliance.
The Flagged Student wanted a conversation before any referral. The integrity officer pointed out the university requires reporting every suspected violation.
How polished your writing is, writing in a second language, using a grammar or translation tool, or using an approved accommodation is never grounds for a question and never evidence in one.
The TA seat priced the original at 23 hours a semester to enforce as written. The teacher would have spent zero, because nobody does.
Does it say what counts as AI? If the word “Grammarly” isn’t in it, the answer is probably no.
